content: Infection with enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is a frequent cause of diarrhoea in both adults and children in developing countries. It is also a significant cause of travellers' diarrhoea in individuals visiting or returning from regions where ETEC is endemic. A killed whole-cell vaccine, Dukoral®, which was originally designed and licensed to prevent cholera, has been suggested by some groups as a potential preventive measure for travellers' diarrhoea. This vaccine includes a recombinant B subunit of cholera toxin, which is antigenically similar to the heat-labile toxin produced by ETEC. The purpose of this review was to assess the clinical efficacy of Dukoral® and other vaccines specifically developed to protect against ETEC-related diarrhoea. The objective of the review was to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity of vaccines designed to prevent diarrhoea caused by ETEC infection. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to December 2012. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared the use of vaccines for ETEC prevention with no intervention, a control vaccine (either an inert vaccine or one for an unrelated infection), an alternative ETEC vaccine, or different doses or schedules of the same ETEC vaccine. The participants included healthy adults and children living in endemic regions, those intending to travel to such regions, or volunteers exposed to an artificial ETEC challenge. Two independent authors assessed the eligibility and risk of bias for each trial. Data extraction and analysis were performed using Review Manager (RevMan) software, and outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The review included 24 RCTs with a total of 53,247 participants. Four studies examined the protective efficacy of oral cholera vaccines for preventing ETEC diarrhoea, while seven studies evaluated ETEC-specific vaccines. Of these 11 studies, seven were field trials, and four were artificial challenge studies. An additional 13 trials provided data on safety and immunological outcomes. The oral cholera vaccine Dukoral® was assessed in a single RCT involving travellers from the USA to Mexico. This study did not demonstrate any statistically significant effect on ETEC diarrhoea or all-cause diarrhoea (one trial, 502 participants, low-quality evidence). Two earlier trials, conducted in Bangladesh and among travellers from Finland to Morocco, evaluated a precursor to Dukoral® that contained purified cholera toxin B subunit rather than the recombinant subunit. These trials showed short-term protective efficacy against ETEC diarrhoea lasting approximately three months (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.71; two trials, 50,227 participants). However, this earlier version of the vaccine is no longer available. An ETEC-specific killed whole-cell vaccine, which also included the recombinant cholera toxin B subunit, was evaluated in travellers from the USA to Mexico or Guatemala and from Austria to regions in Latin America, Africa, or Asia. No statistically significant differences were observed in the incidence of ETEC-specific diarrhoea or all-cause diarrhoea (two trials, 799 participants). However, this vaccine was associated with an increased risk of vomiting (RR 2.0, 95% CI 1.16 to 3.45; nine trials, 1,528 participants). Other ETEC-specific vaccines currently under development have not yet demonstrated clinically meaningful benefits. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence from RCTs to support the use of the oral cholera vaccine Dukoral® for preventing ETEC diarrhoea in travellers. Further research is necessary to develop vaccines that are both safe and effective, providing shortand long-term protection against ETEC diarrhoea.
